titre: Wu (1957): The Experiment That Tells Left from Right
accroche: In 1957, the Nobel Prize in Physics crowns the violation of parity. It goes to the two theorists, not to the physicist whose experiment demonstrated it.
contenu_vulgarise:
How do you explain to an inhabitant of a distant star system what we call left and right? Before 1957, it was impossible: no known law of physics distinguished them. The speech presenting the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics uses precisely this example to say what an experiment had just changed.

## A Question Nobody Had Asked

The presentation speech recalls how Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang went about it. Troubling observations on particles called K mesons lead them to ask what experimental support there was for the idea that all processes between particles are symmetric between right and left. Their conclusion, the speech says, is unexpected: even for the best-known processes, none. All the experiments had been set up to give the same result whether the symmetry held or not.

Lee and Yang go further. They publish in *Physical Review* (vol. 104, p. 254, 1956) a review of the data and propose tests. In the summer of 1956, they suggest to Chien-Shiung Wu that she test the beta decay of cobalt-60, according to Wikipedia.

## From Cobalt to a Hundredth of a Kelvin

Wu sets up the experiment at the National Bureau of Standards, with Ernest Ambler, R. W. Hayward, D. D. Hoppes, and R. P. Hudson. Cobalt-60 nuclei, tiny magnets, are aligned by a magnetic field and cooled to near absolute zero, about 0.01 kelvin, by demagnetization of a paramagnetic salt. The goal is to count in which direction the electrons of beta radioactivity fly off, a process governed by the weak interaction, one of the four fundamental interactions.

If left and right were equivalent, as many would fly off upward as downward. The Nobel speech describes the result: with the current running counterclockwise in the coil, the electrons are preferentially thrown toward the floor. The asymmetry appeared in December 1956 according to Wikipedia, and the paper, “Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay,” appears in *Physical Review* on February 15, 1957 (vol. 105, p. 1413).

## The Prize

The 1957 Prize in Physics is awarded half to Yang and half to Lee, “for their penetrating investigation of the so-called parity laws.” The same speech names Wu, and says that she carried out the first of these experiments with her collaborators. She is not among the laureates.

According to Wikipedia, which relies on *Physics World*, she received 23 Nobel nominations, put forward by 18 physicists between 1958 and 1974. In 1978 she receives the first Wolf Prize in Physics. According to the same source, colleagues at Columbia had confirmed the result through separate experiments.

## What the Prize Leaves Out

The result removes something taken for granted: the symmetry between left and right, assumed to hold, does not apply to the weak interaction, something no one had tested. The prize, for its part, honors the theoretical investigation; the experiment that settled the matter appears only in the presentation speech.

What other symmetry still holds for the sole reason that no one has set up the experiment that makes it fail?

carte.punch: 1957: the Nobel crowns the violation of parity. It goes to two theorists, not to Wu.
carte.idee: Lee and Yang propose a test, physicist Chien-Shiung Wu carries it out on cobalt-60 cooled to 0.01 kelvin: the electrons fly off to one side rather than the other. In this decay, left and right are not equivalent. The 1957 Nobel goes to Lee and Yang.

quiz.question: In Wu's experiment, what is observed about the electrons emitted by the aligned cobalt-60 nuclei?
choix: As many electrons fly off in all directions, as symmetry predicts
They all fly off exactly in the direction of the applied magnetic field
More of them fly off one way than the other, which symmetry forbade
They fly off in all directions, but in growing numbers as temperature rises
quiz.explication: With the nuclei aligned by the magnetic field, the electrons are emitted preferentially in one direction, toward the floor in the Nobel speech's description: right-left symmetry is not respected. If they flew off equally in all directions, parity would be conserved. Nor do they all follow the field, and the temperature of the salt is near absolute zero, not high.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who receives the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work on parity?
choix: Ernest Ambler and his NBS collaborators
Lee, Yang, and Wu in equal shares
Chen Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee, half each
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The prize is awarded half to Yang and half to Lee, for their theoretical investigation; Wu, who carried out the experiment, is not among them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To what temperature are the cobalt-60 nuclei cooled in Wu's experiment?
choix: About 0.01 kelvin, close to absolute zero
About 100 kelvins, the temperature of liquid nitrogen
0 degrees Celsius, the temperature of melting ice
The ambient temperature of the laboratory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The nuclei are aligned by a magnetic field and then cooled to about 0.01 kelvin, by demagnetization of a paramagnetic salt, close to absolute zero.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Wikipedia citing Physics World, how many Nobel nominations did Chien-Shiung Wu receive?
choix: None, her name was never put forward
23 nominations, put forward by 18 physicists between 1958 and 1974
More than 50 nominations, a record for a woman scientist
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wikipedia, relying on Physics World, reports 23 nominations put forward by 18 physicists between 1958 and 1974; she never received the prize.
